hints: Recall the colour of aqueous bromine and think about what happens to the C=C double bond when bromine adds across it.
walkthrough:
Picture the test for unsaturation**
You have an alkene, so you have a C=C double bond ready to react. Aqueous bromine, often called bromine water, is naturally an orange or brown solution.

Link addition to colour loss**
When bromine adds across the double bond, the $Br-Br$ molecule is consumed to form a colourless dibromoalkane. Because the coloured bromine disappears, the solution goes from orange / brown to colourless.
Final answer: Orange / brown solution decolourises to colourless.

hints: Learn the cleavage rules for hot, concentrated, acidified $MnO_4^-$: a $=CH_2$ group gives $CO_2$, a $=CH-R$ group gives $RCO_2H$, and a $=C(R)_2$ group gives a ketone.
For X, match $CO_2$ to a $=CH_2$ end and $(CH_3)_2CO$ to a $(CH_3)_2C=$ end, then join the two C atoms of the double bond together.
For Z, note only one carbon product $CH_3CO_2H$ is formed, so the alkene must be symmetrical with identical groups on each side of the C=C bond.
walkthrough:
Use the cleavage rules as a decoder**
Hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) cuts the C=C bond completely. Think of it like this: $=CH_2$ is oxidised all the way to $CO_2$, $=CHR$ becomes $RCOOH$ (a carboxylic acid), and $=CR_2$ becomes $R_2C=O$ (a ketone). You can work backwards from products to the alkene.

Rebuild X**
X gives $CO_2 + (CH_3)_2CO$. $CO_2$ must have come from a $CH_2=$ end. $(CH_3)_2CO$ must have come from a $(CH_3)_2C=$ end. Join those two carbons with a double bond: $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$.

Rebuild Y**
Y gives $CO_2 + CH_3CH_2CO_2H$. Again $CO_2$ means a $CH_2=$ end. $CH_3CH_2CO_2H$ means the other side was $CH_3CH_2CH=$. Join them: $CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$.

Rebuild Z**
Z gives only $CH_3CO_2H$. That acid must have come from a $CH_3CH=$ group. Since only one type of product is seen, both sides of the double bond must be the same. Join two $CH_3CH=$ units: $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$.

hints: Count the carbon and hydrogen atoms in any one of the structures of X, Y or Z you have just drawn, remembering they are isomers.
walkthrough:
Count from your structures**
Take X, $(CH_3)_2C=CH_2$. It has 4 carbons in total and 8 hydrogens. Y, $CH_3CH_2CH=CH_2$, and Z, $CH_3CH=CHCH_3$, both also contain 4 carbons and 8 hydrogens. Since X, Y and Z are isomers, they share the same molecular formula $C_4H_8$.

hints: Focus on the carbon atom bonded to the $OH$ group and count how many other carbon atoms are directly attached to it.
Recall that one attached carbon means primary ($1^\circ$) and three attached carbons means tertiary ($3^\circ$).
walkthrough:
Classify by the C-OH carbon**
Do not just look for an $OH$ group. Look at the carbon carrying it. In V, $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_2OH$, the $CH_2OH$ carbon is joined to only one other carbon, so it is a primary or $1^\circ$ alcohol.

Apply the same test to W**
In W, $(CH_3)_3COH$, the central carbon carrying the $OH$ is joined directly to three $CH_3$ groups, that is three other carbons. That makes it a tertiary or $3^\circ$ alcohol.

Final answer: V: primary ($1^\circ$) alcohol
W: tertiary ($3^\circ$) alcohol

hints: Think of this as an acid metal reaction where the $O-H$ hydrogen is replaced by Na to give an alkoxide plus hydrogen gas, then balance H atoms.
walkthrough:
Write the alkoxide product**
Sodium is reactive enough to remove the hydrogen from the $O-H$ group. V, butan-1-ol, becomes its sodium salt, sodium butoxide: $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_2ONa$. The other product is hydrogen gas, $H_2$.

Balance correctly**
You start with one $O-H$ hydrogen but $H_2$ needs two H atoms. So one mole of alcohol gives half a mole of $H_2$: $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_2OH + Na \rightarrow CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_2ONa + \tfrac{1}{2}H_2$.

hints: Think about which oxidising agent changes colour when it oxidises an alcohol, and which class of alcohol resists oxidation.
Recall the colour change of acidified dichromate(VI) when $Cr(VI)$ is reduced to $Cr(III)$.
Consider why W shows no reaction, linking it to the lack of hydrogen atoms on the carbon bearing the $OH$ group.
walkthrough:
Choose the distinguishing oxidant**
Primary alcohols like V can be oxidised, but tertiary alcohols like W cannot be oxidised because the C-OH carbon has no H to remove. Warm with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is the classic test.

Predict the result for V**
V is oxidised first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid. At the same time orange $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ ($Cr(VI)$) is reduced to green $Cr^{3+}$ ($Cr(III)$). So you see orange to green.

Predict the result for W**
W has no H on the $C-OH$ carbon, so no oxidation occurs and the dichromate stays in the +6 state. You see no change, the solution remains orange.

Final answer: Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $K_2Cr_2O_7 / H^+$ (heat)
Observation with V: orange to green
Observation with W: no change, remains orange
